intro.statement: Private credit has become one of the most important asset classes in institutional portfolios. The fundraising infrastructure supporting most credit managers has not kept pace.

who.title: Managers with a differentiated investment process who need an equally rigorous approach to raising capital.

challenge.title: Why traditional fundraising fails to scale
challenge.body: Differentiated credit managers remain under-allocated — not for lack of merit, but because the capital-raising model hasn't evolved. The constraint is capital formation.

items.title: Fragmented Process
items.body: Capital formation, marketing, and IR operate in silos, cut off from the data that drives conviction.

items.title: Lengthy Timelines

items.title: Generic Investor Outreach
items.body: Broad approaches that ignore investor mandates, timing, and allocation nuance.

items.title: Loss of Focus

hero.title: A process built around how investors decide.
hero.subtitle: We analyze, plan, execute, and sustain — an integrated extension of your business across the full capital lifecycle.

steps.title: Analyze & Frame the Challenge
steps.lead: Institutional, investor-grade diagnosis of your private credit strategy, risk profile, and investment case.
steps.body: We assess how your platform takes risk, where alpha is created, and how governance supports it. The output is an institutional-grade investment case that allocators can underwrite: your portfolio role, return and risk parameters, and a clear decomposition of performance, process, and people.

steps.title: Research & Evaluate the Opportunity
steps.lead: We build the analytical foundation of your fundraising strategy.
steps.body: We map the allocator universe for your strategy — by type, geography and mandate fit — and evaluate where demand, competition and timing align. The output is a target list with conviction behind it, and a clear view of what each allocator will need to see before they commit.

steps.title: Design & Execute the Fundraising Plan
steps.lead: A fund manager-specific plan, built to execute.
steps.body: We design the raise around how your target allocators decide — sequencing, materials, data room and DDQ — then run structured outreach with full pipeline visibility, coordinating introductions, meeting preparation and follow-up cadences throughout.

steps.title: Sustain & Compound Investor Relationships
steps.body: As commitments close, we build the LP communications program that sustains the relationship: onboarding, quarterly reporting and re-up planning — so that the next raise starts from a stronger position than the last.

cards.title: Embedded, not episodic
cards.body: An integrated part of your business — capital formation and IR run as one continuous function. Consistency builds conviction.

cards.title: Selectivity over volume
cards.body: We prioritise relevance over reach — and pause when conditions aren't right. Protecting long-term outcomes, never short-term activity.

timeline.text: months from initial engagement to final close — a typical full-cycle fundraise.

items.q: How many clients do you work with at once?
items.a: A small number by design — typically no more than four active mandates at a time, so that every engagement has partner-level attention throughout.

items.q: Do you work on placement fees or retainer?
items.a: Engagements are structured as embedded advisory mandates with a retainer and success component, aligned to the fundraising timeline rather than individual closes.

items.q: How long does a typical fundraise take?
items.a: A full-cycle institutional raise typically runs 18 to 36 months from initial engagement to final close, depending on strategy, track record and target allocator base.

items.q: Do you work with emerging managers or only established firms?
items.a: Both. The constraint is a differentiated, institutional-quality strategy and a willingness to build the process infrastructure the raise requires.
We have allocator relationships in Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and North America. Coverage depth varies by region — we discuss geographic strategy as part of the diagnostic.

items.title: Repositioning a German private credit manager for Northern European institutions
items.subtitle: How we rebuilt the narrative and outreach for a DACH direct-lending specialist and opened Scandinavian, Benelux and UK allocators.
items.challenge: A specialist direct lending manager operating primarily in the DACH region had a strong track record in subordinated corporate loans but limited visibility outside its domestic allocator base. The strategy was differentiated — regional depth, relationship-driven origination, low leverage — but the materials and outreach approach had not been built for international institutional audiences.

approach.title: Structured outreach
approach.body: Configured a CRM and executed a six-month outreach calendar, coordinating and supporting all first- and second-level meetings.

items.outcome: Outcome figures pending client review and confirmation. The engagement established a Northern European allocator pipeline and a materials suite calibrated for international institutional diligence.

items.title: How allocator due diligence has changed for private credit managers
items.subtitle: The operational due diligence process has become as rigorous as investment due diligence. Credit managers who underinvest in their IR infrastructure are paying for it in extended close timelines.
items.h2: The structural shift: operational diligence in parallel with investment diligence
items.p1: The private credit due diligence process has undergone a structural shift since 2020. What was once primarily an investment-led evaluation — returns, track record, team — now involves a parallel operational assessment that many managers are unprepared for.
items.p2: Allocators at institutional quality — pension funds, insurance companies, sovereign wealth funds — now routinely request evidence of CRM systems, LP reporting infrastructure, and compliance documentation before proceeding past a first meeting.
items.quote: Managers who cannot provide this documentation are screened out, regardless of investment quality.
items.p3: The practical response is to build the infrastructure before the raise — a configured CRM, a documented reporting cadence and a DDQ library — so that the operational track moves as quickly as the investment track.

items.title: The European LP landscape for private credit: what has changed
items.subtitle: European pension and insurance allocators increased private credit allocations through 2024. The resulting competition for relationships has raised the bar for how managers present themselves.
toc: What the bar looks like now
items.h2: Allocations through 2024: yield, illiquidity premium and low volatility
items.p1: European institutional allocators increased their private credit allocations meaningfully through 2024, driven by attractive all-in yields relative to public credit and the persistent appeal of illiquidity premiums in a low-volatility context.
items.p2: The competitive consequence is that managers seeking European LP relationships are now competing against a well-organised field of global brands and specialist boutiques.
items.quote: The era of a relationship and a good pitch deck being sufficient has ended.
items.p3: Managers entering Europe should expect a longer diligence cycle, a more structured materials request and a stronger preference for demonstrated process over relationship alone.

items.title: Why positioning is the most under-invested capability in credit fundraising
items.subtitle: Most credit managers have a genuine edge in investment — and struggle to translate it into language that institutional allocators find compelling. The gap is narrower than it appears.
items.h2: Two audiences: investment teams write for portfolio managers, IR teams write for allocators
items.p1: Investment teams write for portfolio managers. Investor relations teams write for allocators. Most credit managers have only the first, and the translation problem shows up immediately in every allocator conversation.

stats.label: Audience most decks are written for

items.p2: The gap between a compelling investment thesis and a compelling fundraising narrative is not about quality of the underlying strategy. It is about audience calibration.
items.quote: The CIO of a European pension fund evaluates managers on different dimensions than a credit-specialist portfolio manager.
items.p3: A positioning framework — differentiation, portfolio role, and risk narrative written for the decision-maker — is the highest-leverage investment most managers have not yet made.
